metaDescription: Five portable tablet stands compared on folded size, weight, base stability and device range, for travel bags, bedside tables and the kitchen counter.
introParagraphs: A portable tablet stand has to do two jobs that pull against each other: fold small enough for a bag and still stand firmly once it is open. The picks here show the spread. The Anozer folds to pocket size with a weighted 322 gram base, the LISEN weighs 15.2 ounces, and the werfami is a 4-in-1 aluminum design that also carries laptops.

Device range matters as much as portability. The Amazon Basics stand holds 4 to 10 inch devices, the generic ABS stand covers 7 to 10.2 inches with 0 to 180 degree adjustment, and the Anozer extends its height from 3.16 to 6.26 inches (8.18 inches overall). Those numbers tell you whether a stand will hold an e-reader on a nightstand or a full tablet on a hotel desk.

We evaluated each pick based on product specs and buyer feedback, ranking the stands on how reliably they stay put, how little they weigh, and how easy they are to set up with one hand. The sections below translate that into scenario-based advice for travelers, bedside readers and anyone who moves a tablet from room to room.

products.name: Anozer Foldable Tablet Stand
products.description:
The Anozer Foldable Tablet Stand pairs a pocket-size fold with a weighted metal base, which is the combination most portable stands miss. The base is 5.55 by 3.94 inches and weighs 322 grams, which gives it a planted feel that thin folding stands lack. Height extends from 3.16 to 6.26 inches, with the whole stand reaching up to 8.18 inches.

The extra base weight is the tradeoff. It makes the stand heavier in a bag than a plastic folding stand, but it also means a tap on the screen does not tip it. It suits people who read or watch video on a desk and want a tidy, stable setup that still travels.

Setup is simple: unfold, extend, set an angle. It folds fully for storage, and the metal can be wiped clean. Compared with the LISEN, it is more compact and has a heavier base, while the Amazon Basics is lighter but offers a smaller device range.
products.bestFor: Travelers who want stability and a pocket-size fold
cons: Small base can feel tight with big tablets

products.name: LISEN Foldable iPad Stand

specList.label: Adjustment
specList.value: Height and angle with bridge screw

products.description:
The LISEN Foldable iPad Stand folds flat for travel and weighs 15.2 ounces, or 0.95 pounds. Instead of clips or magnets it relies on a gravity-based system, where the tablet leans back against the stand and its own weight holds it. A bridge screw adjustment truss rod keeps it stable once extended.

That design makes it quick to use because you simply lean the tablet in. The tradeoff is that you must place it with care, since the hold depends on back tilt and a decent grip surface. It fits people who want a larger-device stand that does not fuss with grips.

At 0.95 pounds it is heavier than the Amazon Basics, but its structure feels more substantial. Folding flat makes it slide into a laptop sleeve. Compared with the Anozer, it is a bit bulkier when packed, while it is easier to set up quickly.
products.bestFor: Larger tablets and quick, clip-free setup
pros: Folds flat for bags and sleeves
cons: At 0.95 lb it is not the lightest option
Needs a firm surface and correct back tilt

products.name: Amazon Basics Multi-Angle Portable Stand

specList.label: Compatibility
specList.value: Kindle, iPhone, iPad, Galaxy Tab and more

products.description:
The Amazon Basics Multi-Angle Portable Stand holds 4 to 10 inch tablets, e-readers and phones for hands-free viewing. A convenient side button releases the hinge so you can move through multiple angles. It holds devices in either portrait or landscape position.

It is the straightforward, no-frills option here, and that is a real benefit for buyers who find fiddly screws and rods annoying. The 10 inch ceiling means large tablets are out, and a plain folding hinge lacks the weight of the Anozer. It suits e-readers, phones and small tablets best.

It packs small and light, and there is nothing to assemble. Wipe it down occasionally to keep the grips clean. Compared with the generic ABS stand, it carries a recognizable brand and a clear compatibility list, while the LISEN handles bigger devices.
products.bestFor: E-readers, phones and small tablets on the go
pros: Clear list of compatible device brands
cons: Limited to devices up to 10 inches
No weighted base for firm taps

products.name: Adjustable Foldable ABS Tablet Stand
products.description:
This adjustable foldable stand is made from ABS plastic and supports tablets from 7 to 10.2 inches. It adjusts from 0 to 180 degrees and supports vertical and horizontal viewing. Slip pads keep the device and the stand in place.

It is the lowest-cost pick here, and that shows in the lightweight plastic build. For occasional use on a nightstand or tray it does the job, but a heavy tablet in a thick case will test the hinges. It suits people who want a spare stand for a travel bag.

Plastic is easy to wipe clean and it adds little weight. Check that the stand locks firmly at your preferred angle before relying on it. Compared with the Anozer, it lacks the weighted base, and compared with the Amazon Basics it has a narrower brand-name pedigree but a slightly wider range up to 10.2 inches.
products.bestFor: A spare travel stand on a tight budget
cons: Plastic hinges may loosen with heavy tablets
Brand and support are less established

products.name: werfami 4-in-1 Aluminum Stand
products.description:
The werfami stand turns from a laptop riser into a tablet easel, a magnetic desk phone holder and more. An integrated N52 magnetic core snaps onto iPhone 12 through 15 models and MagSafe cases. The body is aerospace aluminum alloy that holds 15.6 to 17 inch laptops.

That versatility is the draw and also the compromise. It is a more substantial piece of kit than a simple tablet holder, so it costs more and takes more bag room. It suits remote workers who need one stand for a laptop, a tablet and a phone.

Aluminum cleans easily and resists scratches. Learn the folding sequence once and it becomes second nature. Compared with the Anozer, it is a bigger and more complex stand, while the LISEN is simpler if you only need a tablet.
products.bestFor: Travelers who carry a laptop, tablet and phone
pros: Also works as a laptop riser

buyingCriteria.explanation: The LISEN weighs 15.2 ounces and folds flat, while the Anozer folds fully to pocket size with a 322 gram base. The Amazon Basics and the ABS stand are plastic and lighter in a bag. Measure the pocket or sleeve you plan to use and compare with the folded dimensions, since portability is useless if the stand does not fit. A rule of thumb is to accept extra weight only if it buys real stability, as the Anozer base does.

A weighted base such as the Anozer 5.55 by 3.94 inch metal base resists tipping when you tap the screen. Plastic stands like the ABS pick rely on slip pads and a wide stance. Research on stands notes that heavier devices and cases may need a heavier base, so match the base to your tablet. If you type or draw on the screen, favor the Anozer or LISEN over lightweight plastic.

Supported ranges differ widely: the Amazon Basics covers 4 to 10 inches, the ABS stand 7 to 10.2 inches, and the werfami works with laptops up to 17 inches. Typical stands top out near 11 to 13 inches, so check your tablet with the case on. A stand sized too small will wobble and one sized too large will not grip. Buy for the largest device you plan to use.

The Amazon Basics changes angle with a side button, while the LISEN uses a bridge screw rod and the ABS stand adjusts from 0 to 180 degrees. Senior users rarely get this documented, so test one-handed adjustment and look for joints that hold position without drooping. Fiddly screws can be a deal breaker for stiff hands. Prefer a single-motion hinge if you adjust often.

The LISEN uses a gravity-based system with no clips or magnets, while others use rubber or slip pads. Clips can scratch screens, and magnets only suit compatible devices such as the werfami's MagSafe mount. Gravity systems rely on back tilt and a firm surface. Pick the grip that matches whether you use a case.

The Anozer extends to 8.18 inches overall, which helps raise a screen toward eye level, while most other portable stands sit low. Keeping the screen higher reduces neck strain, though a portable stand rarely gets as high as a desk model. For long sessions, pair a taller stand with a desk. For short viewing, lower is fine.

howWeEvaluated.title: Portability
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared folded size and weight across the group, from the LISEN at 15.2 ounces to the plastic Amazon Basics. The Anozer ranked highest because it folds to pocket size while keeping a heavy base. The bulkiest is the werfami.

howWeEvaluated.title: Stability when open
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at base weight and structure, such as the Anozer 322 gram base and the LISEN truss rod. Plastic hinge stands scored lower for firm tapping. Our assessment is based on specs and buyer feedback.

howWeEvaluated.title: Device compatibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched each stand's range, from the Amazon Basics at 4 to 10 inches to the werfami at laptop sizes. Case allowance was also considered. The widest fit for tablets is the LISEN.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ease of setup
howWeEvaluated.description: We favored one-motion adjustments like the Amazon Basics side button over multi-step folds like the werfami. Gravity-based holds on the LISEN reduce fuss. The strongest overall setup is on the Anozer, and the most involved is the werfami.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value for the price tier
howWeEvaluated.description: The ABS stand is the lowest-cost pick, while the werfami sits at the premium end with extra functions. We favored picks whose cost matched their stability.

cards.label: Weighted base
cards.text: The Anozer with its 322 gram base and the werfami aluminum body stay planted when you tap or type. They weigh more in a bag. They suit desk and hotel table use.

cards.label: Lightweight frame
cards.text: The Amazon Basics and ABS stands are plastic and light, and the LISEN is 0.95 pounds. They are easier to carry. They can tip or slip with heavy tablets.

howToChoose.note: Choose the Anozer for stability and the Amazon Basics for the lightest carry.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A small footprint, a low angle you can see lying down, and a grip that will not slide on a nightstand. Lighter devices such as e-readers need less base weight.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Amazon Basics suits 4 to 10 inch e-readers and tablets with its side-button angles. The Anozer is the better choice if your tablet is heavier and you want a firm base.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You travel often or use a laptop too. The Anozer adds a weighted base and the werfami adds laptop and MagSafe support.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You need an occasional spare stand. The ABS stand is the lowest-cost pick and the Amazon Basics covers e-readers well.

faq.q: How do I choose between a gravity-based stand and a clip stand?
faq.a: A gravity-based stand such as the LISEN leans the tablet back against the frame, so there are no clips to scratch the screen. A clip or pad design holds the device edge more firmly. Choose gravity for speed and clip-free setup, and a grip design if you carry the stand in a moving bag.

faq.q: How much should a portable tablet stand cost?
faq.a: Prices here run from the lowest-cost ABS stand to the premium werfami. You mostly pay for materials and extra functions, not for brand. A mid-range stand like the Amazon Basics or Anozer is enough for most readers.

faq.q: How do I keep a portable stand in good shape?
faq.a: Wipe the hinges and pads occasionally and avoid forcing a joint past its stop. Fold it fully before packing so it does not catch on other items. Replace the stand if a hinge no longer holds an angle.

faq.q: Will a lightweight stand tip over?
faq.a: It can with a large tablet or firm tapping. The Anozer adds a 322 gram base specifically to avoid that, while plastic stands rely on slip pads. Use lighter stands with e-readers and phones, and heavier bases with tablets.
Yes. Cases add thickness and weight, and manufacturers note heavier devices or cases may need a heavier base. Check the supported range, such as 4 to 10 inches on the Amazon Basics, with the case on.

Only if you actually use the extra modes. The werfami also serves as a laptop riser and a magnetic phone holder, which makes sense for remote workers. If you only need a tablet stand, a simpler option is lighter and cheaper.
